finding: model.json keys map to columns by exact, case-sensitive pl.col(name) lookup with no validation, so the train->predict contract is enforced only by the rulebook text (train.py does not exist yet). Measured in scratch/check3_keys.py on edge_predict: (a) ODS-truncated 20-char names, as written in model_coefficients.csv (11 of the 18 effects are longer than 20, e.g. credit_utilization_c, flag_multiple_delinq) -> ColumnNotFoundError; (b) upper-case names -> ColumnNotFoundError (SAS names are case-insensitive, the item store is not); (c) an 'Intercept' entry inside coefficients, as ParameterEstimates lists it -> ColumnNotFoundError; (d) top-level 'Intercept' -> KeyError; (e) a null estimate -> TypeError; (f) duplicate JSON keys -> last value wins silently. Answer to 'is raising what SAS PLM does': for a variable ABSENT from the score data, SAS PLM SCORE stops the step with an ERROR and writes no OUT= data set (my understanding; not verifiable here without SAS), so failing loudly is the right kind of behaviour, and the port must never skip or zero-fill an unknown key (that would silently change pd). For a MISSING VALUE in a present variable, PLM gives a missing prediction, which the port reproduces (5,881 empty pd on edge_predict, verified). So 'missing key raises' is not wrong. The latent problem is that nothing guarantees train writes full, exact-case names. Full names with intercept-only (S8, coefficients={}) work correctly
